The Free Tier Is a Constraint, Not a Discount

Every project that builds against a free API tier eventually makes the same mistake: it treats the quota as a discount on the paid tier rather than as a hard design constraint in its own right. The two produce very different architectures.

A discount mindset says "call the model once per chunk, it is basically free, we will upgrade later if it becomes a problem." A constraint mindset asks, before writing a line of pipeline code, how many requests a single item can possibly cost, and treats any answer above one or two as a bug to be batched away, not a scaling problem to be solved after launch.

In practice this means one structured call per item that returns everything the downstream pipeline needs in one shot — summary, tags, topic, and any kind-specific fields — instead of a chain of five small calls that each do one thing tidily. It means relation labeling happens in a batched sweep across many pending pairs, not one request per pair. And it means the system has to stay useful when the quota is exhausted: search, capture, and extraction all have to keep working on zero budget, with only the LLM-touched stages pausing until the counter resets.

None of this is about being clever with the model. It is about refusing to let a shared, finite resource be spent implicitly, one convenient little call at a time, until the day it quietly runs out mid-afternoon and nobody can explain why.
